opus-5.5.text:
I think Yuandong is one of the people in the field whose taste I really resonate with, and I've learned a lot just from watching how he picks problems. What I admire most is that he's never satisfied with "it works." When something works in deep learning, whether it's self-supervised learning without negative pairs or the way transformers pick up structure during training, his instinct is to ask *why* and to go after the mechanism. He'll take a phenomenon everyone is using and try to write down the training dynamics, sometimes in a very simplified setting, until the behavior falls out of the math. That's a very physicist-like attitude, even though he isn't formally trained as a physicist, and it's very close to what I mean by Science of AI.

For me, Science of AI means treating neural networks as natural objects worth studying in their own right, the way a physicist studies a gas or a biologist studies a cell. You observe phenomena, you build minimal models that reproduce them, and you try to find principles that generalize. Yuandong's work is a great example of the "minimal model plus dynamics" part of that program. You strip away everything inessential, keep the piece that produces the phenomenon, and then you can actually say something precise.

Where we differ a little is more emphasis than philosophy. Yuandong tends to go deeper on the theoretical side. He's comfortable doing quite heavy analysis of gradient dynamics, and I think that rigor is valuable. My own style is often more exploratory and phenomenological. I like to start with toy experiments, visualize what the network is doing, find something surprising, like grokking or the emergence of structured representations, and only then ask what theory would explain it. Sometimes I'm closer to an experimental physicist, and he's closer to a theorist. But I think the field needs both, and the best work happens when they meet in the middle.

The other thing I appreciate about him is that he connects understanding back to building. He doesn't treat understanding as a purely academic exercise. If you really understand why something works, you should be able to design a better algorithm or a more efficient architecture. I share that belief strongly. A lot of people see interpretability or theory as a luxury, something you do after the engineering is done. I think it's the opposite. As models get bigger and more expensive, trial and error becomes very costly, and understanding becomes a competitive advantage.

So I'd say his taste and mine sit in the same broad family: curiosity-driven, mechanism-seeking, and grounded in simple models. It's encouraging to see someone with that taste do impactful work at the frontier, because it shows this kind of research isn't just a side hobby. It can actually shape where AI goes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Yuandong and I actually share a lot of the same instinct, even though we come at it from different angles. He's someone who has spent years inside large-scale industrial systems, training real models at Meta, and yet he keeps going back to the question of "why does this work?" rather than just "does this work?" That's rare. Most people in that position stay on the engineering side because that's where the rewards are. He insists on understanding the mechanism, on finding the mathematical structure underneath, and I really respect that.

For me, Science of AI is about treating neural networks as a natural phenomenon, something we observe, probe, and try to explain, almost the way a physicist approaches a new material. My background is physics, so my taste is toward simple toy models, phase transitions, scaling laws, interpretability, things like KAN where you try to make the structure legible. Yuandong's taste is closer to what I'd call a theorist with an engineer's grounding. He'll take a real transformer, look at the training dynamics, and try to derive what the attention layers are actually learning, with actual theorems where he can get them.

So the overlap is that we both believe understanding is not a luxury, it's a prerequisite for the next jump. Scaling alone won't tell you when you'll hit a wall or how to go around it. The difference is maybe in scale and in idealization. I'm comfortable studying a tiny network on modular arithmetic for months if it reveals a clean principle. He tends to want the explanation to survive contact with a real system at scale. Honestly I think the field needs both. The toy model gives you the hypothesis, the large-scale work tests whether the hypothesis is real or just an artifact of simplicity.

If anything, talking with people like him pushes me to ask whether my pretty pictures actually hold up when the model has billions of parameters. And I hope the reverse is true too, that the physics-style approach gives people doing large-scale work a vocabulary for what they're seeing. That's really what I mean by Science of AI, building that shared language.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the connection around the kinds of questions we want to ask. Science of AI, to me, means treating AI itself as something to understand: Why does a system learn certain things? What determines its behavior? Can we turn an observation into a principle that makes predictions?

I don’t want to speak for Tian Yuandong’s research taste, but the overlap I’d look for is a desire to get beneath performance and understand the mechanism. There can still be a difference in emphasis: you might start with a practical problem and develop theory to explain it, or start with a puzzling phenomenon and build a simplified setting to study it. Those approaches can reinforce each other. The important thing is that the explanation eventually comes back into contact with what the system actually does.

sol-6.1.text: I think there’s a natural overlap, especially in wanting to understand why learning works rather than only showing that it works. But I can’t speak for Yuandong’s motivations. The way I’d frame my own direction in Science of AI is to treat AI systems as objects of scientific study: find a clear phenomenon, build a simple model, and test whether the explanation actually predicts what happens. Research taste enters in choosing which phenomena are worth explaining and how much complexity you’re willing to strip away. So I’d be interested in that comparison at the level of specific questions, rather than saying our directions are simply the same or different.
